Instead, the focus is on how a bumpy earnings season will continue playing out with many large U.S. companies reporting results. Highlights include Amazon, Microsoft, Coca-Cola, Boeing and Alphabet.  4,028.10 +0.50%   10/26/2026, 6:48:03 AM ET       Monkey see, monkey buy   Five years ago today, Brandon Buchanan ’s investment firm paid a record $3.4 million for a drawing of a primate.

   Feel free to gaze at his or any of the 9,999 other JPEGs in the Bored Ape Yacht Club. You can even make a copy for personal use, but officially owning one on the blockchain will cost you. The “best offer” for Buchanan’s is about 97% lower than in 2021, which is typical.

   To most people, Bored Apes and their nonfungible token brethren, such as Pudgy Penguins and CryptoPunks, are a curiosity. Their wild rides hold some useful investing lessons, though, such as what made them so valuable in the first place.

   One is “social proof.” Celebrities endorsing a product is an age-old tactic, but buying one with their own money creates its own kind of validation. And many of the news stories about Justin Bieber, Snoop Dogg, Paris Hilton and Jimmy Fallon’s Bored Apes mentioned specific dollar amounts paid (in cryptocurrency equivalent).

   Once broadcast, they seemed reasonable. That can anchor our price expectations for speculative stocks, but it’s especially relevant when valuing something like art that will never produce cash flows.

   Then there’s identity. Some buyers consider meme stocks or crypto as a sort of initiation into a group—an emotionally appealing feature cleverly tapped with the apes’ “club” moniker. “We’re part of the same community,” said Fallon to Hilton as they compared apes on “The Tonight Show.”

   They were among celebrities sued for failing to disclose financial incentives tied to their ownership (plaintiffs’ case is on weak ground since Bored Apes probably don’t qualify as securities).

   Hype aside, collectibles are a substantial asset class and diversifier among the wealthy, NFTs included. In an email interview, Buchanan points out that tokenized art “can be admired by others, and the transferability is seamless.”

   You might be capable of drawing a nifty cartoon, but good luck selling it on the blockchain. The secret sauce is a combination of buzz and scarcity. There’s only a loose connection between an artwork’s beauty and its price.

   Leonardo da Vinci’s “Salvator Mundi” sold for $125 in 1958 when it was thought to have been painted by a student. Then it smashed price records in 2017, fetching $450 million. Fewer than 20 da Vinci paintings exist.

   People who are passionate about collectibles aren’t as swayed by soaring prices, making buying opportunities rare. Pitching them as an easily-transferable investment short-circuits that, though.

   Buchanan says he’d sell his rare Bored Ape on behalf of his fund if its price rose tenfold, but probably not one he owned personally. He expects them to be shown in museums.

   “I’d hate to see NFTs…just be talked about as monkey photos that people speculated on that went bust.”

   Collectibles can still be a good investment without being investments, and many actual investments can still be bad. The more their value relies on psychological anchors, the greater the chance of them making a monkey out of you.

       Stocks I’m Watching   ↘️   XP , Petrobras ,   MercadoLibre : Shares of the Brazil-linked companies slid after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva  unexpectedly beat out Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s election . U.S.-traded shares of Brazilian financial-services company XP tumbled more than 40% premarket, while state oil company Petrobras’s U.S. shares slid more than 20%. MercadoLibre, an e-commerce and payments company, fell 10% in early trading.

   ↘️   CoreWeave , Nebius ,   Iren : Shares of the so-called neocloud providers fell around 3% premarket. Worries over the sustainability of AI spending have knocked the stocks in recent weeks. Elon Musk yesterday warned that hundreds of neocloud companies could see “ guppy-level death .”

   ↗️   SpaceX : Musk also said on X that his rocket company has closed on $40 billion in debt financing for graphics processing units. Shares rose 1% premarket.

   ↘️   Moderna : Shares fell 5% ahead of the bell, on track to extend last week’s selloff after results from a closely watched cancer vaccine study fell short of investors’ expectations.

   🔎   Verizon ,   Welltower and Whirlpool are among those expected to report earnings today.

       One Big Chart         Turbine maker GE Vernova is an AI stock-market darling. But Siemens Energy, its nearly identical German competitor, is down 1.4% this year and trades at a forward-earnings multiple about 40% lower. The gap is hard to justify .

       What I’m Reading   • So, about that earnings boom: Two AI chip makers are providing one-third of growth for the S&P 500 this quarter. ( WSJ )

   • The U.S. is adding manufacturing jobs again. The catch: You might need a college degree to get one. ( WSJ )

   • Moderna investors should brace for more whiplash. Even after its sharp fall, the drugmaker’s stock price assumes wild success. ( WSJ )

   • Americans have tens of billions of dollars in stranded retirement accounts. ( Barron’s )

   • Chinese companies make lots of things. Increasingly, profits aren’t one of them. ( The Atlantic )

       Today in Markets History   📰 On this day in 1825, the Erie Canal was inaugurated. Financed with $6 million in stock and bonds and eight years in the making, the canal cut shipping time from New York to Buffalo from three weeks to eight days, slashing the cost of transporting goods. The American frontier was opened to a two-way flood of commerce.

Monkey see, monkey buy

 

Five years ago today, Brandon Buchanan’s investment firm paid a record $3.4 million for a drawing of a primate.

 

Feel free to gaze at his or any of the 9,999 other JPEGs in the Bored Ape Yacht Club. You can even make a copy for personal use, but officially owning one on the blockchain will cost you. The “best offer” for Buchanan’s is about 97% lower than in 2021, which is typical.

One is “social proof.” Celebrities endorsing a product is an age-old tactic, but buying one with their own money creates its own kind of validation. And many of the news stories about Justin Bieber, Snoop Dogg, Paris Hilton and Jimmy Fallon’s Bored Apes mentioned specific dollar amounts paid (in cryptocurrency equivalent).

 

Once broadcast, they seemed reasonable. That can anchor our price expectations for speculative stocks, but it’s especially relevant when valuing something like art that will never produce cash flows.

 

Then there’s identity. Some buyers consider meme stocks or crypto as a sort of initiation into a group—an emotionally appealing feature cleverly tapped with the apes’ “club” moniker. “We’re part of the same community,” said Fallon to Hilton as they compared apes on “The Tonight Show.”

 

They were among celebrities sued for failing to disclose financial incentives tied to their ownership (plaintiffs’ case is on weak ground since Bored Apes probably don’t qualify as securities).

 

Hype aside, collectibles are a substantial asset class and diversifier among the wealthy, NFTs included. In an email interview, Buchanan points out that tokenized art “can be admired by others, and the transferability is seamless.”

 

You might be capable of drawing a nifty cartoon, but good luck selling it on the blockchain. The secret sauce is a combination of buzz and scarcity. There’s only a loose connection between an artwork’s beauty and its price.

 

Leonardo da Vinci’s “Salvator Mundi” sold for $125 in 1958 when it was thought to have been painted by a student. Then it smashed price records in 2017, fetching $450 million. Fewer than 20 da Vinci paintings exist.

 

People who are passionate about collectibles aren’t as swayed by soaring prices, making buying opportunities rare. Pitching them as an easily-transferable investment short-circuits that, though.

 

Buchanan says he’d sell his rare Bored Ape on behalf of his fund if its price rose tenfold, but probably not one he owned personally. He expects them to be shown in museums.

 

“I’d hate to see NFTs…just be talked about as monkey photos that people speculated on that went bust.”

 

Collectibles can still be a good investment without being investments, and many actual investments can still be bad. The more their value relies on psychological anchors, the greater the chance of them making a monkey out of you.
